title: Genesis 4:17–26
context: Cain’s line multiplies: a city named for Enoch, generations down to Lamech, polygamy, tents, music, metalwork, and a boast of multiplied vengeance. The chapter then turns back to Adam and Eve: Seth is appointed in Abel’s place, Enosh is born, and people begin to call on the LORD’s name of the Lord.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Classic comment on Cain’s city, Lamech’s boast, and calling on the name of the LORD, from both sides of the debate.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Jabal was a famous shepherd; he delighted much in keeping cattle, and was so happy in devising methods of doing it to the best advantage, and instructing others in them, that the shepherds of those times, nay, the shepherds of after-times, called him Father; or perhaps his children after him, being brought up to the same employment: the family was a family of shepherds. Jubal was a famous musician, and particularly an organist, and the first that gave rules for that noble art or science of music.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Gen 4:19)

reformed.quote: From the context we may gather that Cain, before he slew his brother, had married a wife; otherwise Moses would now have related something respecting his marriage; because it would be a fact worthy to be recorded, that any one of his sisters could be found, who would not shrink with horror from committing herself into the hand of one whom she knew to be defiled with a brother's blood; and while a free choice was still given her, should rather choose spontaneously to follow an exile and a fugitive, than to remain in her father's family. Moreover, he relates it as a prodigy that Cain, having shaken off the terror he had mentioned, should have thought of having children: for it is remarkable, that he who imagined himself to have as many enemies as there were men in the world, did not rather hide himself in some remote solitude.

verses.text: Cain knew his wife. She conceived, and gave birth to Enoch. He built a city, and named the city after the name of his son, Enoch.
verses.arminianNotes:
Life continues for the marked man: a wife, a son, a city named Enoch. Culture rises even among those who have walked from the Lord’s presence.

Achievement is distinct from peace with God. Cities can be built in Nod. Grace still allows family and work; it does not baptize distance from the Lord as safety.
verses.reformedNotes:
Providence preserves Cain’s household. A city appears early—human making under a curse, named for a son. Common life is not snuffed out.

God restrains chaos enough for civilization to start, even east of Eden. That is common grace, not proof that Cain’s way has become the way of life.

verses.text: Irad was born to Enoch. Irad became the father of Mehujael. Mehujael became the father of Methushael. Methushael became the father of Lamech.
verses.arminianNotes:
Names pass down to Lamech. Generations accumulate without the text pausing to praise their faith. Lineage can carry either worship or wound.

History is morally weighted. Each generation remains responsible before God; a famous ancestor neither saves nor dooms a child who must still answer grace.
verses.reformedNotes:
The genealogy is spare and purposeful: it runs to Lamech, where the line’s character will show. God records what He will later contrast with Seth.

Providence writes family trees. The Lord of history is not absent from Cain’s descendants even when the narrative withholds revival.

verses.text: Lamech took two wives: the name of the first one was Adah, and the name of the second one was Zillah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Lamech takes two wives—the first polygamy in Scripture, a departure from the one-flesh pattern of Genesis 2. The text reports; it does not applaud.

God’s creational design remains the standard. Distorted marriage is a human choice under resistible conscience, not a new command from heaven.
verses.reformedNotes:
Two wives named is not progress; it is fracture of the Edenic pattern. Lamech’s house already tells on his heart.

After the fall, desire rewrites God’s gifts. Common life continues, but the shape of the household now advertises autonomy rather than covenant fidelity.

verses.text: Adah gave birth to Jabal, who was the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jabal fathers tent-life and herding. Skills that can serve neighbor and worship also appear in Cain’s line. Culture is not cursed as such.

God lets good arts arise among mixed people. Those gifts should be received with gratitude and used under His moral will, not as a rival salvation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Pastoral and nomadic crafts have a “father.” Genesis honors skill without confusing it with holiness.

Reformed doctrine of common grace: the Lord distributes making and herding even where saving faith is not the theme. Culture can be gift while the heart remains unreconciled.

verses.text: His brother’s name was Jubal, who was the father of all who handle the harp and pipe.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jubal fathers lyre and pipe. Music enters the record as human joy and craft. Beauty can praise God or decorate pride.

The same grace that gives song invites its use in calling on the Lord (v. 26). Instruments do not save; they can serve love or Lamech’s boast.
verses.reformedNotes:
Music too is fathered in this line. The Creator’s world still yields melody after murder and exile.

Common grace includes the arts. Lyre and pipe are not Seth’s monopoly; God is generous with gifts He will one day reclaim for true worship.

verses.text: Zillah also gave birth to Tubal Cain, the forger of every cutting instrument of bronze and iron. Tubal Cain’s sister was Naamah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Technology arrives—tools that can till or kill. Naamah’s naming reminds us daughters belong in the story too.

Skill is morally open. Forging is a trust; people remain accountable for whether metal serves life or multiplies Lamech’s violence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Metallurgy is credited to Tubal-cain; Naamah is remembered by name. Genesis will not let culture be anonymous, nor only male.

God allows the age of bronze and iron to dawn in a restless line. Providence governs the tools of history long before Israel’s law will regulate their use.

verses.text: Lamech said to his wives, “Adah and Zillah, hear my voice. You wives of Lamech, listen to my speech, for I have slain a man for wounding me, a young man for bruising me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Lamech turns violence into a song. A wound is answered with a killing; a strike with a young man’s death. The song teaches his wives to admire excess.

Culture without repentance curdles. Music and metal now soundtrack revenge. Grace still names this as sin to be refused, not as fate to be sung.
verses.reformedNotes:
The first poem after Eden is a taunt of blood. Lamech inflates injury into license to kill. Art becomes propaganda for the self.

When God is not feared, strength writes its own law. This is the seed of Cain matured—sin crouching, then composing.

verses.text: If Cain will be avenged seven times, truly Lamech seventy-seven times.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Cain’s protective sevenfold becomes Lamech’s seventy-sevenfold boast. Mercy is twisted into a brand. He claims a vengeance God never assigned him.

Arminians see responsible escalation. God’s kindness to Cain was meant to restrain killing; Lamech resists that intent and multiplies harm by choice.
verses.reformedNotes:
Lamech takes over God’s own number. What was the Lord’s deterrent for Cain becomes a human claim to unlimited payback.

Jesus will later invert seventy-seven into forgiveness (Matt 18:22). Here the line of Cain baptizes revenge; only grace can break the math.
verses.keyContrast: Both refuse Lamech’s boast as distortion of God’s mark on Cain. Arminians underline a resistible misuse of mercy Lamech chose; Reformed readers stress the deep bondage and pride of a line God still limits even as it hymns its own wrath.

verses.text: Adam knew his wife again. She gave birth to a son, and named him Seth, saying, “for God has given me another child instead of Abel, for Cain killed him.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The camera returns to Adam and Eve. Seth is appointed in place of Abel. Eve reads the birth as God’s answer to murder, not as chance.

God sincerely continues the promise of offspring (3:15). He appoints a line through which grace will keep offering life; hearers are summoned to trust that appointment rather than Cain’s city.
verses.reformedNotes:
Seth’s name is theology: God appointed another seed. The promise does not die in Abel’s field. Eve interprets history by God’s act, not by Lamech’s song.

Comfort: election of a line here is mercy after blood. The Lord preserves the offspring through whom He will bring the Serpent-crusher, and He does it as appointment, not accident.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear Eve’s appointed as God’s faithful answer to Abel’s death. Arminians underline ongoing, sincere provision of a promised seed people may trust; Calvinists emphasize God’s sovereign appointment of the line He will keep for redemption.

verses.text: A son was also born to Seth, and he named him Enosh. At that time men began to call on the LORD’s name.
verses.arminianNotes:
Enosh is born, and public worship surfaces: people begin to call on the LORD’s name of the Lord. Against Lamech’s voice, another voice rises—prayer, not boast.

Arminian readers treasure this as grace restoring true religion in history. Calling on the Lord is a human act enabled from above; the name is offered to be invoked, and the church still lives by that call.
verses.reformedNotes:
A son, then a liturgy. “Call on the LORD’s name” is the first note of gathered worship in Genesis—the opposite of Nod’s self-song.

God not only appoints Seth; He grants a people who invoke His name. True worship is His gift in a violent world, the line along which promise will travel until the better blood speaks.
